issues.legal_issue: The three-year restriction on considering a landlord’s bona fide-requirement ground bars consideration on the merits before the restricted period expires, but does not bar filing the application earlier.
material_facts: The premises were occupied by a sitting tenant when the landlord purchased them.
The landlord filed an application relying on bona fide requirement before three years had elapsed from the purchase.
The authority considered the bona fide-requirement ground on the merits after three years had elapsed from the purchase.
issues.conclusion: The application was not barred by the three-year restriction because the authority considered the bona fide-requirement ground on the merits only after the restricted period had expired; the resulting decree was not a nullity.
issues.legal_principle: Under the first proviso to Section 21(1) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, “entertained” means taken up for consideration and adjudication on the merits, not instituted or filed. The statutory scheme supports that distinction. Lakshmiratan Engineering Works Ltd. v. Asst. Commissioner (Judicial) and Hindustan Commercial Bank Ltd. v. Punnu Sahu explain that “entertain” means to adjudicate upon or proceed to consider on the merits. Anandilal Bhanwarlal v. Smt. Kasturi Devi Ganeriwala was distinguishable because the provision there prohibited institution of a suit. The general rule that a decree made without jurisdiction is a nullity, stated in Kiran Singh v. Chaman Paswan and reiterated in Chiranjilal Shrilal Goenka v. Jasjit Singh, did not apply because the authority considered the ground after the required period had elapsed.

predicates.possession_proceeding_on_bona_fide_need: A landlord sought possession of rented premises on the ground of the landlord’s bona fide need.
predicates.premises_had_sitting_tenant_when_purchas: The premises were occupied by a tenant when the landlord purchased them.
predicates.application_filed_before_waiting_period_: The landlord filed the application before the required post-purchase waiting period had elapsed.
predicates.waiting_period_elapsed_before_merits_con: The authority took up the bona fide-need ground for consideration on the merits after the required post-purchase waiting period had elapsed.

issues.definition: When a possession proceeding based on bona fide need concerns premises purchased with a sitting tenant, an early filing is not barred if the required waiting period has elapsed before the authority considers the ground on its merits.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant may waive a mandatory notice-period protection intended for the tenant’s personal benefit by abandoning the objection and proceeding on the merits.
material_facts: The landlord filed the possession application before six months had elapsed from the notice seeking possession.
The tenant raised the premature-filing objection in its written statement but did not pursue it afterward.
The tenant joined issue on the merits, including by seeking cross-examination on the landlord’s claimed need, and did not raise the objection in the appeal before raising it later.
The landlord lost the opportunity to withdraw the proceeding and seek permission to bring a fresh one after the notice period, and would have been prejudiced by the late objection.
issues.conclusion: Although the six-month notice requirement was mandatory, the tenant waived its protection by consciously abandoning the objection and litigating the merits; the tenant was also precluded from raising the objection late after the landlord’s position had irretrievably changed.
issues.legal_principle: The first proviso to Section 21(1) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 requires the landlord to give at least six months’ notice before filing an application on the bona fide-requirement ground. The Court treated this mandatory protection as personal to the tenant and capable of waiver, rather than a prohibition serving public interest. Krishan Lal v. State of J&K supports waiver of a mandatory provision designed to safeguard an individual’s interest. Vellayan Chettiar v. Government of the Province of Madras and Dhirendra Nath Goral v. Sudhir Chandra Ghosh likewise support waiver of protections personal to a party. The principle in Surajmull Nargoremuil v. Triton Insurance Company, approved in Seth Badri Prasad v. Seth Nagarmal, that a statutory prohibition cannot be cured by consent or failure to plead, did not govern because this provision afforded personal protection rather than imposing a prohibition in the public interest. The lost opportunity to seek withdrawal and permission to file afresh under Order XXIII Rule 1(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure, and the resulting prejudice, also supported the conclusion.

rule.if: possession_proceeding_on_bona_fide_need and notice_period_incomplete_at_filing and tenant_raised_but_abandoned_objection and tenant_litigated_on_merits and landlord_prejudiced_by_late_objection

predicates.possession_proceeding_on_bona_fide_need: A landlord sought possession of rented premises on the ground of the landlord’s bona fide need.
predicates.notice_period_incomplete_at_filing: The landlord filed the application before the required notice period had elapsed.
predicates.tenant_raised_but_abandoned_objection: The tenant initially objected to premature filing but did not pursue that objection afterward.
predicates.tenant_litigated_on_merits: The tenant proceeded to contest the landlord’s claim on its merits.
predicates.landlord_prejudiced_by_late_objection: The tenant’s late objection deprived the landlord of an earlier opportunity to withdraw and pursue a fresh proceeding after the notice period.

issues.definition: A tenant waives a personal notice-period protection when, in a possession proceeding based on bona fide need, the tenant abandons the premature-filing objection, litigates the merits, and a late objection would prejudice the landlord.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s bona fide need is not defeated merely because the landlord resides in adjoining property in which the landlord’s spouse has an undivided interest.
material_facts: The landlord had no property of his own in the town and was staying in the adjoining part of the building where the rented premises were situated.
The adjoining property was not the spouse’s exclusive property but was jointly owned by the spouse and the spouse’s brother.
The landlord’s bona fide need for the rented premises had been found on the evidence by the courts below.
issues.conclusion: The spouse’s undivided interest in the adjoining property did not defeat the landlord’s bona fide need for the rented premises.
issues.legal_principle: In determining bona fide need under Section 21(1)(a) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, the subsequent circumstance must be assessed in context. A landlord with no home of his own in the town could not be compelled to remain as a licensee in property that was not exclusively owned by the spouse but was jointly owned with another person. The Court upheld the concurrent factual findings of bona fide need.

rule.if: possession_proceeding_on_bona_fide_need and landlord_bona_fide_need_established and landlord_has_no_own_home_in_town and landlord_stays_in_spouse_co_owned_property

predicates.possession_proceeding_on_bona_fide_need: A landlord sought possession of rented premises on the ground of the landlord’s bona fide need.
predicates.landlord_bona_fide_need_established: The evidence established the landlord’s bona fide need for the rented premises.
predicates.landlord_has_no_own_home_in_town: The landlord had no home of the landlord’s own in the town.
predicates.landlord_stays_in_spouse_co_owned_proper: The landlord stayed in property in which the spouse had only a shared ownership interest with another person.

issues.definition: A spouse’s shared ownership of the residence where the landlord stays does not defeat an established bona fide need when the landlord has no home of the landlord’s own in the town.

issues.legal_issue: The deemed-sufficiency rule for a retired service member’s residential need does not apply when the building was not let by that landlord before retirement.
material_facts: The landlord was a retired army officer.
The landlord purchased the rented building after retiring and had not let it out before retirement.

The High Court treated the landlord’s representation of residential need as deemed sufficient under the statutory explanation, but the landlord’s counsel accepted that this reasoning was unsustainable.
issues.conclusion: The statutory deemed-sufficiency reasoning did not apply because the landlord had not let the building before retirement, although the independently established bona fide need remained sufficient to sustain the possession decree.
issues.legal_principle: Explanation (iii) to Section 21(1) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 deems a serving or retired Indian soldier’s representation of residential need sufficient only where the building was let out before the landlord’s retirement and the landlord needs it for residential occupation by himself or his family. The condition concerning letting before retirement was not met.

predicates.possession_proceeding_on_bona_fide_need: A landlord sought possession of rented premises on the ground of the landlord’s bona fide need.
predicates.landlord_is_retired_service_member: The landlord was a retired member of the armed forces.
predicates.building_not_let_by_landlord_before_reti: The landlord had not let the building before retiring from service.

issues.definition: In a possession proceeding based on bona fide need, a retired service member does not receive deemed sufficiency of the claimed need if the building was not let by that landlord before retirement.
